title: Electron configuration and quantum numbers
note: Four quantum numbers label each electron: n (shell), l (subshell shape, 0 to n − 1), ml (orientation, −l to +l), and ms (spin, ±½). Electrons fill the lowest-energy subshells first, in the order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p. Each orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin, and equal-energy orbitals fill singly before pairing.

read.title: An address for every electron
text: Quantum mechanics describes electrons in atoms with four quantum numbers, which work like an address. The principal quantum number n names the shell; larger n means a larger, higher-energy shell. The second number, l, can run from 0 up to n − 1 and names the subshell: 0 is s, 1 is p, 2 is d, and 3 is f. The magnetic number ml picks one orbital within the subshell, so a p subshell has three orbitals and a d subshell has five. The spin number ms is either +½ or −½.
No two electrons in an atom can share all four numbers. That rule, the Pauli exclusion principle, limits every orbital to two electrons with opposite spins.

To build a ground-state configuration, add electrons to the lowest-energy subshell available. The order is not simply by shell: 4s fills before 3d, which is why potassium's last electron goes into 4s. Within a subshell, electrons spread out over the orbitals before pairing, so nitrogen has three unpaired 2p electrons. A few elements break the expected pattern, such as chromium and copper, where a half-filled or filled d subshell gives a lower energy. When transition metals form cations, they lose their outer s electrons first.
